answerHtml:
Here are the results:

Flash-Flood Risk for Jizan — 2025-08-23

Probability: 12.53% (low risk) - Model verified ROC-AUC: 0.873 (highly reliable model)

Why this risk exists

The physical mechanisms driving flash-flood risk in Jizan are:

  • Active Red Sea Trough (ARST) — A low-pressure trough over the Red Sea that draws in moist air. When it interacts with eastward-moving Mediterranean cyclones and the Arabian Anticyclone, it can produce intense rainfall. *(de Vries et al., 2013)*

  • Moisture Transport — Surface fluxes over the Red Sea supply low-level moist air, contributing ~30–40% of regional rainfall. Stronger winds can enhance latent heat fluxes, fueling convection. *(ResearchGate case study; MDPI Atmosphere, 2019)*

  • Orographic Lift — The Hejaz/Asir mountains force moist air upward, enhancing rainfall on the windward side (where Jizan is located).

    • Recommendation

    The risk on August 23 is low (~12.5%), so no major concern. However, Jizan is climatologically prone to flash floods during the summer monsoon season (July–September) due to the Red Sea Trough and orographic effects. Keep an eye on short-term forecasts if you're planning activities in wadi (valley) areas.

🌪️ Dust Storm Risk – Dammam, 2025-07-06

Probability: 90.3% — Very High Risk

This is based on a verified model (ROC-AUC = 0.8866), using indicators from 2025-07-05.

What the indicators showed on July 5th

- 10m wind speed: 9.0 m/s - 850 hPa wind speed: 18.4 m/s (strong low-level winds) - Wind shear (850–200 hPa): 26.69 m/s - Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD): 4.54 kPa (very dry air) - Temperature max: 39.3°C - No precipitation — dry surface conditions

The independent rule-based detection engine also flagged elevated risk (score 0.6), confirming consistent elevated risk between the model and physical indicators.

🏙️ Context

Dammam has a population of ~1.57 million (2022 census), so this is a significant urban area at risk.

What Physically Causes Dust Storms in Saudi Arabia

The primary mechanism is the Summer Shamal — a persistent north-northwesterly wind regime that dominates from May to August. It is driven by:

  • Thermal low (desert heat low) — Intense surface heating over the Arabian Peninsula creates a deep low-pressure system.
  • Steep pressure gradient — Between the heat low over Pakistan/Afghanistan/Iran and high pressure over the eastern Mediterranean and northern Saudi Arabia.
  • Strong low-level winds (especially at 850 hPa and 10 m) lift loose, dry desert dust into the atmosphere.
  • Low humidity / high VPD — Dry conditions keep dust particles suspended longer.

    • Key citation: *Yu et al. (2016), J. Geophys. Res. Atmos.* — "The summer Shamal, occurring from May to August, is a persistent north-northwesterly wind regime driven by high pressure over eastern Africa and thermal low-pressure centres over Iran and Pakistan."

    ✅ Recommendation

    Given the >90% probability, strong winds, and very dry conditions, residents and authorities in Dammam should prepare for likely dust storm conditions on July 6th — reduced visibility, potential impacts on transportation (especially at King Fahd International Airport and on Gulf roads), and health precautions for those with respiratory conditions.

🔬 What Drove This Forecast

Jizan (pop. ~174,000, 2022 census) sits at just 7.7 m elevation on the Red Sea coast, making it highly exposed to wadi flooding.

Key indicators from 2025-03-26 that fed the model: - CAPE (convective available potential energy): 1,336 J/kg — strong instability - PWAT (precipitable water): 40.7 mm — deep moisture column - IVT (integrated vapor transport): 54.4 kg/m/s — moisture flux from the Red Sea

Physical mechanisms (from the causal knowledge graph):

  • Active Red Sea Trough (ARST) — low-level convergence over the Red Sea, drawing moisture northward (de Vries et al., 2013)
  • Moisture transport from the Red Sea and Arabian Sea — surface fluxes regulate pre-convection convergence (ResearchGate case study; MDPI Atmosphere, 2019)
  • Orographic lift over the nearby Asir mountains (though Jizan itself is coastal flatland)

    • ⚠️ Caveat: The independent rule-based detection engine did *not* flag the same elevated risk (score: 0.25 vs. model's 0.94), noting that classic physical thresholds weren't fully met. The model may be picking up a subtle signal the simpler check misses — treat with added caution.

    🧭 Recommendation

    Residents and authorities in Jizan should prepare for possible flash flooding and wadi overflow on March 27. Monitor Saudi NCM bulletins, avoid low-lying areas and dry riverbeds (wadis), and be ready to move to higher ground if rain intensifies.

answerHtml:
Here are the flash flood forecast model's reliability metrics:

Flash Flood Forecast Model — Verification Scores

Threshold-Independent (Overall Skill)

- ROC-AUC: 0.873 — This is strong. It means the model ranks risky days above non-risky days 87.3% of the time, regardless of where you set the decision threshold.

Threshold-Dependent Metrics (at operational threshold = 0.5)

These are the scores at the fixed threshold the system uses to decide whether to issue an alert:

MetricValueWhat it means
POD (Probability of Detection)0.1004 (≈10%)Only ~10% of actual flash-flood days are correctly flagged. The model misses ~90% of real events.
FAR (False Alarm Ratio)0.8026 (≈80%)Of all alerts issued, ~80% are false alarms. Only ~20% of alerts correspond to an actual event.
CSI (Critical Success Index)0.0713 (≈7%)A combined measure — only 7% of "flagged or observed" days are correct hits.
HSS (Heidke Skill Score)0.1301 (≈13%)Modest improvement over random chance (0 = no skill, 1 = perfect).

Why Are These Scores So Low?

Flash floods are extremely rare events in Saudi Arabia. When a hazard is rare, even a well-calibrated model (ROC-AUC = 0.87) will have low POD and high FAR at a fixed threshold, because:

- The model is conservative — it only raises the flag when it's very confident (threshold 0.5). - Most days are non-event days, so even a small false-alarm rate produces many false alarms in absolute terms. - The ROC-AUC (0.87) tells you the model *ranks* risk well, but the threshold-based scores reflect the inherent difficulty of predicting rare, high-impact convective events.

Bottom Line

The model is good at distinguishing risky from non-risky conditions overall (ROC-AUC 0.87), but at its operational threshold it catches only ~1 in 10 real flash-flood events and ~80% of its alerts are false alarms. This is a known challenge for rare-hazard forecasting — not a broken model. If you want higher detection, the threshold could be lowered, but that would increase false alarms further.
